newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Credit Lyonnais salvage plan may be close.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Credit Lyonnais salvage plan may be close.

text.p: Agreement was reported near on a new salvage plan for ailing state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais on Thursday but the French finance ministry would not confirm any progress.
A "consensus is developing" in government circles to help the bank, said a source close to negotiations between the government and Credit Lyonnais.
The talks are aimed at saving the bank from an ignominious plunge back into the red as a result of a state bailout last year that has gone badly awry.
The solution was said to centre on bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade's favoured option which would free the bank of the financial burden of helping finance its own rescue.

The government and the bank, bailed out by the state in 1994 and 1995, have been in a race against time to come up with new salvage terms before Credit Lyonnais' board meets on September 26 to approve its half-year results.

Business daily Les Echos reported on Thursday Peyrelevade had written a letter to the government vowing to quit unless accord was reached by Friday but it added the threat was unlikely to be carried out as progress was being made.

The source close to the talks said the letter was written in July when discussions were deadlocked. "I doubt he will resign because he knows things are coming to a solution. Things are going quite quickly."
The afternoon daily Le Monde also reported a deal was close and said the main stumbling block was the 10 billion French francs ($2 billion) it would cost the deficit-fighting government this year.

But a source close to the government said there was no truth to Le Monde's report. Separately, the finance ministry would only say the two sides were "working every day" to reach a solution "because one must be found".

Credit Lyonnais racked up losses of 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994 as a result of a reckless expansion spree that briefly turned it into the world's largest bank outside Japan. It eked out a 13 million franc profit in 1995.
Banking analysts have said unless last year's rescue terms are revised, the bank could tip back into loss this year.

Under the 1995 rescue, it transferred 130 billion francs of shaky assets to a state-backed rescue vehicle, the Public Body for Financing and Restructing, known as the EPFR and gave the state a 119 billion franc loan to finance the acquisition.

But to get Credit Lyonnais to share the pain of its rescue, and to get the bailout approved by European Union competition authorities in Brussels, the government dictated that the bank lend the 119 billion francs at below-market interest rates.
The bank has ended up paying twice as much to fund the loan as it collects in interest payments and in France's morose banking climate, it has been unable to make up the shortfall.
It says the gap will cost it three billion francs this year -- which analysts calculate could push it into a two billion franc loss for the year.
The source close to the talks said removing the burden of the state rescue loan from Credit Lyonnais would "allow it to go forward, free from the burden of the past."

Any solution, however, would have to be approved by the European Commission. Les Echos suggested the commission could lay down new conditions for its approval or demand a commitment by the government to speed up privatisation of the bank.

The finance ministry recently asked justice officials to probe whether charges could be laid against against the bank's former bosses over its huge past losses. French newspapers speculated at the time the move was a bid to soften up taxpayers for the announcement of a new salvage package for the bank. ($1=5.080 French Franc)
